nameStory: The Common Murre gets its name from being the most widespread and frequently seen member of the murre family. The word 'murre' likely comes from their distinctive low, purring calls that echo across their clifftop colonies. They're also called guillemots in some places, from the French name 'guillemot' referring to their pointed bills.
description: Common Murres are large, penguin-like seabirds that spend most of their lives on the ocean. These stocky birds are excellent underwater swimmers, using their wings like flippers to 'fly' through the water while hunting fish. They're about the size of a small duck but much more robust, with dark backs and white bellies. You'll typically see them floating in groups on the water or diving beneath the surface rather than flying overhead.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Stocky, torpedo-shaped body that looks built for diving, with a thick neck and compact appearance when floating on water

idTips.label: Coloring
idTips.description: Dark chocolate brown to black back and head with bright white belly and chest, creating a sharp contrast like a tuxedo

idTips.label: Bill
idTips.description: Straight, pointed black bill that looks like a dark dagger - perfect for catching slippery fish underwater

idTips.label: Swimming Behavior
idTips.description: Sits low in the water and disappears completely when diving, often popping up far from where they went down

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies in straight lines with rapid wingbeats close to the water surface, looking somewhat labored and direct

idTips.label: Group Behavior
idTips.description: Almost always seen in flocks or groups, rarely alone, often forming loose rafts of dozens of birds on the water

habitat: In New England waters, Common Murres are found offshore in deeper ocean areas, particularly around fishing banks and upwelling zones where fish are abundant. They prefer cooler waters and are most commonly spotted from ferries, whale watching boats, or rocky headlands along the Maine coast. During winter, they may move closer to shore but rarely come into shallow bays or harbors.

seasonality.spring: Murres begin returning to offshore New England waters in late spring as they finish their breeding activities further north. You might spot them during migration as they move through area waters.
seasonality.summer: Generally absent from New England waters during peak summer as they're busy breeding on northern cliffs in Canada and other Arctic regions.
seasonality.fall: Start appearing in New England waters in larger numbers during fall migration, often seen in mixed flocks with other seabirds moving south.
seasonality.winter: Most commonly observed in New England during winter months when they're in their non-breeding areas, floating in offshore waters and diving for fish.

funFact: Common Murre chicks make one of the most daring leaps in the bird world - at just 20 days old and still unable to fly, they jump off 400-foot cliff faces and glide down to the ocean below, accompanied by their devoted fathers who will continue caring for them at sea!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Thick-billed Murre, but Common Murres have thinner, more pointed bills without the white line along the bill edge that Thick-billed Murres show. Remember: 'Common' has a 'clean' bill, while Thick-billed has that telltale white stripe.
contextualKnowledge: Common Murres are sometimes called 'guillemots' in Europe and eastern Canada, which can be confusing since we also have different birds called Black Guillemots in New England waters. The term 'murre' is more commonly used in North America to distinguish them from the smaller, different-looking Black Guillemot.
compareHints: Common Murres are much more likely to be seen in New England than their close relative, the Thick-billed Murre. The Common Murre's bill is noticeably thinner and more pointed, while the Thick-billed Murre has a deeper, more triangular bill with a distinctive white stripe along the cutting edge. Common Murres also tend to prefer slightly warmer waters than their thick-billed cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Common Murre, the Thick-billed Murre has a noticeably more robust, triangular bill versus the Common Murre's longer, thinner bill.
